claim: Plexins are semaphorin receptors that play essential roles in mammalian neuronal axon guidance.
source: Plexins are semaphorin receptors that play essential roles in mammalian neuronal axon guidance and in many other important mammalian biological processes.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about plexins.

claim: Plexins play essential roles in many other important mammalian biological processes.
source: Plexins are semaphorin receptors that play essential roles in mammalian neuronal axon guidance and in many other important mammalian biological processes.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Plexin signaling depends on a semaphorin-induced dimerization mechanism.
source: Plexin signaling depends on a semaphorin-induced dimerization mechanism and is modulated by small GTPases of the Rho family, of which RND1 serves as a plexin activator yet its close homolog RhoD an inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Plexin signaling is modulated by small GTPases of the Rho family.
source: Plexin signaling depends on a semaphorin-induced dimerization mechanism and is modulated by small GTPases of the Rho family, of which RND1 serves as a plexin activator yet its close homolog RhoD an inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: RND1 serves as a plexin activator.
source: Plexin signaling depends on a semaphorin-induced dimerization mechanism and is modulated by small GTPases of the Rho family, of which RND1 serves as a plexin activator yet its close homolog RhoD an inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript (Zanata et al., 2002).

claim: RhoD is a plexin inhibitor.
source: Plexin signaling depends on a semaphorin-induced dimerization mechanism and is modulated by small GTPases of the Rho family, of which RND1 serves as a plexin activator yet its close homolog RhoD an inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript (Zanata et al., 2002).

claim: RhoD is a close homolog of RND1.
source: Plexin signaling depends on a semaphorin-induced dimerization mechanism and is modulated by small GTPases of the Rho family, of which RND1 serves as a plexin activator yet its close homolog RhoD an inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and established knowledge.

claim: RND1 reinforces the plexin dimerization interface.
source: Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we showed that RND1 reinforces the plexin dimerization interface, whereas RhoD destabilizes it due to their differential interaction with the cell membrane.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RhoD destabilizes the plexin dimerization interface.
source: Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we showed that RND1 reinforces the plexin dimerization interface, whereas RhoD destabilizes it due to their differential interaction with the cell membrane.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RND1 and RhoD have differential interactions with the cell membrane.
source: Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we showed that RND1 reinforces the plexin dimerization interface, whereas RhoD destabilizes it due to their differential interaction with the cell membrane.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon binding plexin at the RBD, RND1 and RhoD interact differently with the inner leaflet of the cell membrane.
source: Upon binding plexin at the Rho-GTPase-binding domain (RBD), RND1 and RhoD interact differently with the inner leaflet of the cell membrane and exert opposite effects on the dimerization interface via an allosteric network involving the RBD, RBD linkers, and a buttress segment adjacent to the dimerization interface.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RND1 and RhoD exert opposite effects on the dimerization interface via an allosteric network involving the RBD, RBD linkers, and a buttress segment adjacent to the dimerization interface.
source: Upon binding plexin at the Rho-GTPase-binding domain (RBD), RND1 and RhoD interact differently with the inner leaflet of the cell membrane and exert opposite effects on the dimerization interface via an allosteric network involving the RBD, RBD linkers, and a buttress segment adjacent to the dimerization interface.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: RhoD features a short C-terminal tail.
source: The differential membrane interaction is attributed to the fact that, unlike RND1, RhoD features a short C-terminal tail and a positively charged membrane interface.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and structural data.

claim: RhoD features a positively charged membrane interface.
source: The differential membrane interaction is attributed to the fact that, unlike RND1, RhoD features a short C-terminal tail and a positively charged membrane interface.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and simulation data.

claim: RND1 does not feature a short C-terminal tail like RhoD.
source: The differential membrane interaction is attributed to the fact that, unlike RND1, RhoD features a short C-terminal tail and a positively charged membrane interface.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: There are nine plexin family members including plexin A1–4, B1–3, C1, and D1.
source: Plexins are a family of nine single-pass transmembrane receptor proteins including plexin A1–4, B1–3, C1, and D1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the plexin family.

claim: Plexins are single-pass transmembrane receptor proteins.
source: Plexins are a family of nine single-pass transmembrane receptor proteins including plexin A1–4, B1–3, C1, and D1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plexin structure.

claim: Plexins are best known as the receptors of extracellular semaphorin ligands.
source: Plexins are best known as the receptors of extracellular semaphorin ligands (Nishide and Kumanogoh, 2018) that are guidance cues for neuronal axons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nishide and Kumanogoh, 2018.

claim: Semaphorin ligands are guidance cues for neuronal axons.
source: Plexins are best known as the receptors of extracellular semaphorin ligands (Nishide and Kumanogoh, 2018) that are guidance cues for neuronal axons.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Plexins help regulate cell migration, angiogenesis, and immune responses.
source: Plexins also help regulate other essential biological processes such as cell migration, angiogenesis, and immune responses (Sakurai et al., 2012; Takamatsu and Kumanogoh, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sakurai et al., 2012 and Takamatsu and Kumanogoh, 2012.

claim: Aberrant plexin activity is associated with neurological disorders and cancer metastasis.
source: Aberrant plexin activity is associated with a plethora of diseases including neurological disorders and cancer metastasis (Gu and Giraudo, 2013; Tamagnone, 2012; Yaron and Zheng, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gu and Giraudo, 2013; Tamagnone, 2012; Yaron and Zheng, 2007.

claim: Plexin architecture is conserved across the family.
source: Plexin architecture is conserved across the family.
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and citations.

claim: Plexin consists of a large multi-domain extracellular module including the ligand-binding Sema domain.
source: Plexin consists of a large multi-domain extracellular module including the ligand-binding Sema domain, a single-pass transmembrane helix, and an intracellular module that includes a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain and a Rho-family GTPase-binding domain (RBD) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and Figure 1A.

claim: Plexin consists of a single-pass transmembrane helix.
source: Plexin consists of a large multi-domain extracellular module including the ligand-binding Sema domain, a single-pass transmembrane helix, and an intracellular module that includes a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain and a Rho-family GTPase-binding domain (RBD) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and Figure 1A.

claim: Plexin intracellular module includes a GAP domain and an RBD domain.
source: Plexin consists of a large multi-domain extracellular module including the ligand-binding Sema domain, a single-pass transmembrane helix, and an intracellular module that includes a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) domain and a Rho-family GTPase-binding domain (RBD) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and Figure 1A.

claim: In plexin signaling, semaphorin binds at the extracellular module, which leads to activation of the GAP domain.
source: In plexin signaling, semaphorin binds at the extracellular module, which leads to activation of the GAP domain.
evidence: This is supported by structural and functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: A semaphorin dimer interacts with two plexins at the extracellular module.
source: Structures (Janssen et al., 2010; Kuo et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010) showed that a semaphorin mediates plexin dimerization: a semaphorin dimer interacts with two plexins at the extracellular module, and this extracellular dimerization leads to dimerization at the intracellular module (Figure 1B), and in turn activation of the GAP domain for the substrate Rap GTPases (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies (Janssen et al., 2010; Kuo et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010) and Figure 1B.

claim: Extracellular dimerization of plexin leads to dimerization at the intracellular module.
source: Structures (Janssen et al., 2010; Kuo et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010) showed that a semaphorin mediates plexin dimerization: a semaphorin dimer interacts with two plexins at the extracellular module, and this extracellular dimerization leads to dimerization at the intracellular module (Figure 1B), and in turn activation of the GAP domain for the substrate Rap GTPases (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and Figure 1B.

claim: Plexin dimerization leads to activation of the GAP domain for the substrate Rap GTPases.
source: Structures (Janssen et al., 2010; Kuo et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2010; Nogi et al., 2010) showed that a semaphorin mediates plexin dimerization: a semaphorin dimer interacts with two plexins at the extracellular module, and this extracellular dimerization leads to dimerization at the intracellular module (Figure 1B), and in turn activation of the GAP domain for the substrate Rap GTPases (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012 and Figure 1B.

claim: The dimerization stabilizes the active conformation of the activation segments of the GAP domains.
source: The dimerization stabilizes the active conformation of the so-called activation segments of the GAP domains, which otherwise adopts an inactive conformation that precludes Rap binding to the GAP domain (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Without dimerization, the activation segments adopt an inactive conformation that precludes Rap binding to the GAP domain.
source: The dimerization stabilizes the active conformation of the so-called activation segments of the GAP domains, which otherwise adopts an inactive conformation that precludes Rap binding to the GAP domain (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: The GAP activity switches off the signaling of plexin substrate Rap by catalyzing its GTP hydrolysis.
source: In plexin signaling, the GAP activity switches off the signaling of plexin substrate Rap by catalyzing its GTP hydrolysis and converting it from the GTP-bound state to the GDP-bound state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GAP function.

claim: GAP activity converts Rap from the GTP-bound state to the GDP-bound state.
source: In plexin signaling, the GAP activity switches off the signaling of plexin substrate Rap by catalyzing its GTP hydrolysis and converting it from the GTP-bound state to the GDP-bound state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GAP function.

claim: The RBD of plexin B1 binds Rac1, Rac2, Rac3, Rnd1, Rnd2, Rnd3, and RhoD.
source: The RBD of plexin B1 has been shown to bind Rac1, Rac2, Rac3, Rnd1, Rnd2, Rnd3, and RhoD, but not RhoA, Cdc42, RhoG, or Rif (Fansa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fansa et al., 2013.

claim: The RBD of plexin B1 does not bind RhoA, Cdc42, RhoG, or Rif.
source: The RBD of plexin B1 has been shown to bind Rac1, Rac2, Rac3, Rnd1, Rnd2, Rnd3, and RhoD, but not RhoA, Cdc42, RhoG, or Rif (Fansa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fansa et al., 2013.

claim: Rho-family GTPases serve as regulators in plexin activation.
source: These Rho-family GTPases to various degrees serve as regulators in plexin activation.
evidence: This is supported by functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Overexpression of Rac1 leads to higher cell surface expression of plexin.
source: Overexpression of Rac1 leads to higher cell surface expression of plexin and enhances plexin interaction with semaphorin, suggesting that Rac1 acts as an upstream activator of plexin (Vikis et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vikis et al., 2002.

claim: Overexpression of Rac1 enhances plexin interaction with semaphorin.
source: Overexpression of Rac1 leads to higher cell surface expression of plexin and enhances plexin interaction with semaphorin, suggesting that Rac1 acts as an upstream activator of plexin (Vikis et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vikis et al., 2002.

claim: Rac1 acts as an upstream activator of plexin.
source: Overexpression of Rac1 leads to higher cell surface expression of plexin and enhances plexin interaction with semaphorin, suggesting that Rac1 acts as an upstream activator of plexin (Vikis et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Vikis et al., 2002.

claim: Binding of overexpressed RND1 to plexin triggers cell collapse in the absence of semaphorin.
source: Binding of overexpressed RND1 to plexin triggers cell collapse in the absence of semaphorin, suggesting that RND1 is a more potent activator than Rac1 for plexin (Zanata et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zanata et al., 2002.

claim: RND1 is a more potent activator than Rac1 for plexin.
source: Binding of overexpressed RND1 to plexin triggers cell collapse in the absence of semaphorin, suggesting that RND1 is a more potent activator than Rac1 for plexin (Zanata et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Zanata et al., 2002.

claim: Simultaneous extracellular binding of semaphorin and intracellular RBD binding of certain regulatory GTPases appear to be a prerequisite for full activation of at least some plexins.
source: Simultaneous extracellular binding of semaphorin and intracellular RBD binding of certain regulatory GTPases appear to be a prerequisite for full activation of at least some plexins (Bell et al., 2011), but RBD binding with some other regulatory GTPases of the Rho family attenuates plexin activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bell et al., 2011.

claim: RBD binding with some regulatory GTPases of the Rho family attenuates plexin activity.
source: Simultaneous extracellular binding of semaphorin and intracellular RBD binding of certain regulatory GTPases appear to be a prerequisite for full activation of at least some plexins (Bell et al., 2011), but RBD binding with some other regulatory GTPases of the Rho family attenuates plexin activity.
evidence: This is supported by functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: RhoD binds plexin RBD with similar affinity as RND1.
source: RhoD binds plexin RBD with similar affinity as RND1 (Fansa et al., 2013), but it strongly inhibits plexin signaling (Zanata et al., 2002) rather than activates it.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fansa et al., 2013.

claim: RhoD strongly inhibits plexin signaling.
source: RhoD binds plexin RBD with similar affinity as RND1 (Fansa et al., 2013), but it strongly inhibits plexin signaling (Zanata et al., 2002) rather than activates it.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zanata et al., 2002.

claim: Rho-family GTPases do not alter the GAP activity of plexin in solution in either the monomeric or the active dimer state.
source: Activity assays in solution showed that the Rho-family GTPases do not alter the GAP activity of plexin either in the monomeric or the active dimer state (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: RND1 is anchored to the membrane by a C-terminal amphipathic helix.
source: RND1 is anchored to the membrane by a C-terminal amphipathic helix (Figure 1C) and RhoD by lipidation of a cysteine at the C-terminal tail (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the membrane may play an important role in their plexin regulation.
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and Figure 1C.

claim: RhoD is anchored to the membrane by lipidation of a cysteine at the C-terminal tail.
source: RND1 is anchored to the membrane by a C-terminal amphipathic helix (Figure 1C) and RhoD by lipidation of a cysteine at the C-terminal tail (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the membrane may play an important role in their plexin regulation.
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The membrane may play an important role in plexin regulation by RND1 and RhoD.
source: RND1 is anchored to the membrane by a C-terminal amphipathic helix (Figure 1C) and RhoD by lipidation of a cysteine at the C-terminal tail (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the membrane may play an important role in their plexin regulation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the membrane anchoring of these GTPases.

claim: Resolved complex structures of plexin RBD with different Rho-family GTPases showed that the RBD binds with these GTPases in a similar mode.
source: Resolved complex structures of plexin RBD with different Rho-family GTPases, such as RND1 (PDB 2REX and 3Q3J) and Rac1 (Wang et al., 2012), showed that the RBD binds with these GTPases in a similar mode.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from PDB entries and citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: The binding mode of RhoD with plexin RBD is similar to other Rho-family GTPases.
source: The structure of plexin RBD in complex with RhoD is not available, but data from NMR chemical shift analyses as well as binding assays with RhoD in different nucleotide states and mutants of plexin RBD together suggested that the binding mode is similar (Fansa et al., 2013; Tong et al., 2007; Zanata et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Fansa et al., 2013; Tong et al., 2007; Zanata et al., 2002.

claim: The RBD domain does not undergo substantial or global conformational changes upon binding with Rho-family GTPases.
source: The crystal structures and other biophysical data all suggest that the RBD domain does not undergo substantial or global conformational changes upon binding with Rho-family GTPases (Bell et al., 2011; Tong et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bell et al., 2011; Tong et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Modulations of plexin activity from Rho-family GTPases are unlikely to be mediated by major conformational changes within the RBD domain.
source: Modulations of plexin activity from Rho-family GTPases thus are unlikely to be mediated by major conformational changes within the RBD domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data.

claim: The crystal structure of the RhoD/plexin B2-RBD complex was determined.
source: To understand the apparent paradox regarding the antithetic effects of RND1 and RhoD on plexin activation, we determined the crystal structure of the RhoD/plexin B2-RBD complex, which confirmed that the RBD binding mode of RhoD is similar to that of other Rho-family regulatory GTPases.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The RBD binding mode of RhoD is similar to that of other Rho-family regulatory GTPases.
source: To understand the apparent paradox regarding the antithetic effects of RND1 and RhoD on plexin activation, we determined the crystal structure of the RhoD/plexin B2-RBD complex, which confirmed that the RBD binding mode of RhoD is similar to that of other Rho-family regulatory GTPases.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: RND1 binding is compatible with the dimerization of plexin A4.
source: The simulations suggested that RND1 binding is compatible with the dimerization of plexin A4 while RhoD binding is likely disruptive to the dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: RhoD binding is likely disruptive to the dimerization of plexin A4.
source: The simulations suggested that RND1 binding is compatible with the dimerization of plexin A4 while RhoD binding is likely disruptive to the dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: RND1 interacts with the membrane loosely and its long C-terminal tail serves as a flexible tether to the membrane.
source: The simulations generated two distinct modes of interactions of RND1 and RhoD with the membrane: RND1 interacts with the membrane loosely and its long C-terminal tail serves as a flexible tether to the membrane (Figure 1D), whereas RhoD interacts with the membrane in a specific manner using a positively charged membrane interface (Figure 1E), which is absent in RND1.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 1D.

claim: RhoD interacts with the membrane in a specific manner using a positively charged membrane interface.
source: The simulations generated two distinct modes of interactions of RND1 and RhoD with the membrane: RND1 interacts with the membrane loosely and its long C-terminal tail serves as a flexible tether to the membrane (Figure 1D), whereas RhoD interacts with the membrane in a specific manner using a positively charged membrane interface (Figure 1E), which is absent in RND1.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 1E.

claim: The positively charged membrane interface is absent in RND1.
source: The simulations generated two distinct modes of interactions of RND1 and RhoD with the membrane: RND1 interacts with the membrane loosely and its long C-terminal tail serves as a flexible tether to the membrane (Figure 1D), whereas RhoD interacts with the membrane in a specific manner using a positively charged membrane interface (Figure 1E), which is absent in RND1.
evidence: This is supported by sequence and structural analysis.

claim: RND1 binding strengthens plexin dimerization by stabilizing the RBD position with respect to the GAP domain.
source: As a result, RND1 binding strengthens plexin dimerization by stabilizing the RBD position with respect to the GAP domain and in turn stabilizing the adjacent dimerization interfaces, while RhoD distorts the RBD position and hinders plexin dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and structural analysis.

claim: RND1 binding stabilizes the adjacent dimerization interfaces.
source: As a result, RND1 binding strengthens plexin dimerization by stabilizing the RBD position with respect to the GAP domain and in turn stabilizing the adjacent dimerization interfaces, while RhoD distorts the RBD position and hinders plexin dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and structural analysis.

claim: RhoD distorts the RBD position and hinders plexin dimerization.
source: As a result, RND1 binding strengthens plexin dimerization by stabilizing the RBD position with respect to the GAP domain and in turn stabilizing the adjacent dimerization interfaces, while RhoD distorts the RBD position and hinders plexin dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and structural analysis.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the crystal contains two RhoD molecules, each of which binds to one plexin B2 RBD molecule.
source: The asymmetric unit of the crystal contains two RhoD molecules, each of which binds to one plexin B2 RBD molecule.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The two RBD domains form a domain-swapped dimer in the structure.
source: Surprisingly, the two RBD domains form a domain-swapped dimer in the structure, with the N-terminal portion of one molecule fold together with the C-terminal portion of the other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The domain-swapped dimer is likely a crystallization artifact.
source: This domain-swapped dimer is likely a crystallization artifact because it cannot form in the context of a plexin dimer (Wang et al., 2013), in which the two RBD domains are far apart from one another (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural constraints and citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: The domain-swapped dimer cannot form in the context of a plexin dimer.
source: This domain-swapped dimer is likely a crystallization artifact because it cannot form in the context of a plexin dimer (Wang et al., 2013), in which the two RBD domains are far apart from one another (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: The two RBD domains are far apart from one another in a plexin dimer.
source: This domain-swapped dimer is likely a crystallization artifact because it cannot form in the context of a plexin dimer (Wang et al., 2013), in which the two RBD domains are far apart from one another (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and Figure 1B.

claim: The structure confirms that RhoD binds the plexin B2 RBD in a mode similar to those of other complexes between Rho-family GTPases and plexin.
source: The structure confirms that RhoD binds the plexin B2 RBD in a mode similar to those of other complexes between Rho-family GTPases and plexin (Bell et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and citations to Bell et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012.

claim: The GTP analogue GMP-PNP and Mg2+ together stabilize the ligand-binding switch I and switch II regions in the active conformation.
source: The GTP analogue GMP-PNP and Mg2+ together stabilize the ligand-binding switch I and switch II regions in the active conformation, which make an extensive interface with one side of the beta-sheet of the RBD (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and Figure 2A, B.

claim: The switch I and switch II regions make an extensive interface with one side of the beta-sheet of the RBD.
source: The GTP analogue GMP-PNP and Mg2+ together stabilize the ligand-binding switch I and switch II regions in the active conformation, which make an extensive interface with one side of the beta-sheet of the RBD (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and Figure 2A, B.

claim: All the residues in RhoD involved in interacting with the RBD are identical between human and mouse RhoD.
source: All the residues in RhoD involved in interacting with the RBD are identical between human and mouse RhoD, suggesting that the cross-species complex that we crystallized is a valid representative of the RhoD/plexin complex.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: The cross-species complex that was crystallized is a valid representative of the RhoD/plexin complex.
source: All the residues in RhoD involved in interacting with the RBD are identical between human and mouse RhoD, suggesting that the cross-species complex that we crystallized is a valid representative of the RhoD/plexin complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation.

claim: The orientation of RhoD and RND1 relative to the RBD domains is slightly different.
source: Interestingly, a superimposition of the RhoD/plexin B2-RBD complex with the RND1/plexin B1-RBD complex based on the RBD domains shows that the orientation of RhoD and RND1 relative to the RBD domains is slightly different (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and Figure 2A, B.

claim: The switch II helix in RhoD is placed further away from the RBD compared with that in RND1.
source: Compared with that in RND1, the switch II helix in RhoD is placed further away from the RBD.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The placement of the switch II helix in RhoD appears to be required to accommodate Phe85, which is bulkier than Cys81, the corresponding RND1 residue.
source: This appears to be required to accommodate Phe85, which is bulkier than Cys81, the corresponding RND1 residue.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The difference in switch II helix placement leads to different pivots of the two GTPases relative to the RBD.
source: This difference leads to different pivots of the two GTPases relative to the RBD, which propagates to a larger difference in the opposite side of the molecule, where the insert helices (αI), a helical segment uniquely present in the catalytic domains of Rho-family GTPases, is located (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and Figure 2A.

claim: The insert helices (αI) are a helical segment uniquely present in the catalytic domains of Rho-family GTPases.
source: This difference leads to different pivots of the two GTPases relative to the RBD, which propagates to a larger difference in the opposite side of the molecule, where the insert helices (αI), a helical segment uniquely present in the catalytic domains of Rho-family GTPases, is located (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rho-family GTPases.

claim: In the context of the active dimer of full-length plexin on the plasma membrane, the αI helix faces the membrane.
source: In the context of the active dimer of full-length plexin on the plasma membrane, the αI helix faces the membrane (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling and Figure 1D, E.

claim: The orientational difference of RhoD and RND1 relative to plexin may affect their interactions with the membrane.
source: This orientational difference of RhoD and RND1 relative to plexin therefore may affect their interactions with the membrane, although it is unclear whether and how that effect is related to the opposite roles of RND1 and RhoD in plexin signaling.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural observations.

claim: Both RBD complexes with RND1 and RhoD are overall stable in simulations.
source: These simulations showed that both complexes are overall stable, with the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of the Cα atoms of the catalytic domains with respect to their initial positions fluctuating around 4 Å when the RBD domain aligned (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 2C.

claim: RND1 appears to be more flexible than RhoD relative to the RBD.
source: By this metric, RND1 appears to be more flexible than RhoD relative to the RBD (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 2D.

claim: The αI helix of RND1 was more flexible than RhoD with respect to the catalytic domain as a whole in the simulations.
source: The αI helix of RND1 was also more flexible than RhoD with respect to the catalytic domain as a whole in the simulations (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 2D, E.

claim: RhoD regulation of plexin activity requires a stable membrane interaction involving the αI helix.
source: This analysis is consistent with our finding that the RhoD regulation of plexin activity requires a stable membrane interaction involving the αI helix, but the RND1 function involves little membrane interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: RND1 function involves little membrane interaction.
source: This analysis is consistent with our finding that the RhoD regulation of plexin activity requires a stable membrane interaction involving the αI helix, but the RND1 function involves little membrane interaction.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data.

claim: RhoD does not alter the GAP activity of plexin A1 in a solvent environment.
source: Previous studies showed that RhoD does not alter the GAP activity of plexin A1 in a solvent environment (Pascoe et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pascoe et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2012.

claim: In the simulations of the RND1-bound dimer, the amphipathic helices at the C-termini of the RND1 molecules remained anchored to the membrane.
source: In the simulations of the RND1-bound dimer, the amphipathic helices at the C-termini of the RND1 molecules remained anchored to the membrane, and the RND1 linkers between the catalytic domains and the amphipathic helices (residues 189–200) are sufficiently long to not affect the position of the catalytic domains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3A.

claim: The RND1 linkers between the catalytic domains and the amphipathic helices are sufficiently long to not affect the position of the catalytic domains.
source: In the simulations of the RND1-bound dimer, the amphipathic helices at the C-termini of the RND1 molecules remained anchored to the membrane, and the RND1 linkers between the catalytic domains and the amphipathic helices (residues 189–200) are sufficiently long to not affect the position of the catalytic domains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3A.

claim: The contact area between the membrane and the RND1 catalytic domains remains relatively small, with a mean at approximately 200 Å2.
source: The contact area between the membrane and the catalytic domains remains relatively small, with a mean at approximately 200 Å2 (Figure 3D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The two RND1 catalytic domains largely remained in their initial positions in simulations.
source: The two RND1 catalytic domains largely remained in their initial positions, with the RMSD of the Cα atoms with respect to their initial positions fluctuating around 6 Å (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3E.

claim: In the simulations of the RhoD-bound plexin dimer, the membrane interactions of the RhoD catalytic domains developed extensive and stable interactions with the membrane.
source: In contrast to the RND1-bound plexin dimer, in the simulations of the RhoD-bound plexin dimer, the membrane interactions of the RhoD catalytic domains developed extensive and stable interactions with the membrane in the courses of the simulations (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The extent of the membrane interaction is closely correlated with the positioning of the catalytic domains in both the RND1- and the RhoD-bound plexin dimers.
source: It is apparent that the extent of the membrane interaction is closely correlated with the positioning of the catalytic domains in both the RND1- and the RhoD-bound plexin dimers.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: With the increase of the membrane interactions, the two RhoD domains deviated substantially from their initial positions.
source: With the increase of the membrane interactions, the two RhoD domains deviated substantially from their initial positions, as shown by the RMSD of Cα atoms with respect to their initial positions (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3E.

claim: The RMSD fluctuation of the RhoD domains was larger than the RND1 domains.
source: The RMSD fluctuation of the RhoD domains was larger than the RND1 domains (Figure 3E), indicating that the differential membrane interactions of RhoD and RND1 lead to their differential positioning and dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3E.

claim: The differential membrane interactions of RhoD and RND1 lead to their differential positioning and dynamics.
source: The RMSD fluctuation of the RhoD domains was larger than the RND1 domains (Figure 3E), indicating that the differential membrane interactions of RhoD and RND1 lead to their differential positioning and dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: For RhoD more than for RND1, the membrane contact area is correlated with the RMSD of the GTPase domain with respect to its initial position.
source: Our analysis showed that, for RhoD more than for RND1, the membrane contact area is correlated with the RMSD of the GTPase domain with respect to its initial position (Figure 3F), in agreement with the notion that the membrane interaction modulates RhoD positioning.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3F.

claim: The membrane interaction modulates RhoD positioning.
source: Our analysis showed that, for RhoD more than for RND1, the membrane contact area is correlated with the RMSD of the GTPase domain with respect to its initial position (Figure 3F), in agreement with the notion that the membrane interaction modulates RhoD positioning.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: RhoD interacts with the membrane with a specific interface involving the αI helix and the α4 helix.
source: Further analysis suggested that RhoD interacts with the membrane with a specific interface involving the αI helix and the α4 helix (Figure 3C); Arg144, Arg145, His154, and Arg155 in this part of RhoD enjoyed stable interactions with the membrane (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3C, G.

claim: Arg144, Arg145, His154, and Arg155 in RhoD enjoyed stable interactions with the membrane.
source: Further analysis suggested that RhoD interacts with the membrane with a specific interface involving the αI helix and the α4 helix (Figure 3C); Arg144, Arg145, His154, and Arg155 in this part of RhoD enjoyed stable interactions with the membrane (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3G.

claim: The RhoD membrane-anchoring interface features pronounced positive electrostatic potential that is favorable for membrane interaction.
source: The RhoD membrane-anchoring interface features pronounced positive electrostatic potential that is favorable for membrane interaction (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and Figure 3G.

claim: The number of RhoD residues in membrane contact grew in the simulations.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, the number of RhoD residues in membrane contact grew in the simulations, and the contact map showed that the membrane contact primarily involved the αI helix (residues 130–146) and its neighboring region.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The membrane contact of RhoD primarily involved the αI helix (residues 130–146) and its neighboring region.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, the number of RhoD residues in membrane contact grew in the simulations, and the contact map showed that the membrane contact primarily involved the αI helix (residues 130–146) and its neighboring region.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Enrichment of negatively charged POPS lipids among the lipids in contact with RhoD developed in the course of the simulations.
source: We also observed the development of enrichment of the negatively charged 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (POPS) lipids among the lipids in contact with RhoD in the course of the simulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), in agreement with the electrostatic nature of the membrane interaction of RhoD.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The enrichment of POPS lipids is in agreement with the electrostatic nature of the membrane interaction of RhoD.
source: We also observed the development of enrichment of the negatively charged 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (POPS) lipids among the lipids in contact with RhoD in the course of the simulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), in agreement with the electrostatic nature of the membrane interaction of RhoD.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: The trend of charged lipids becoming enriched in the membrane interfaces with RhoD molecules was observed in simulations where PIP2 lipids were included in the membrane.
source: The trend of charged lipids becoming enriched in the membrane interfaces with RhoD molecules was also observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) in similar simulations where phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate (PIP2) lipids were included in the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: RND1 interaction with the membrane is much less stable than RhoD, without a specific membrane interface.
source: In contrast, RND1 interaction with the membrane is much less stable, without a specific membrane interface (Figure 3G) and with fewer residues involved (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The positively charged residues in the RhoD membrane interface are almost all replaced in RND1.
source: The positively charged residues in the RhoD membrane interface are almost all replaced in RND1 (Figure 3H), and hence the strong electrostatic feature of RhoD in that region is absent in RND1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and Figure 3H.

claim: The strong electrostatic feature of RhoD in the membrane interface region is absent in RND1.
source: The positively charged residues in the RhoD membrane interface are almost all replaced in RND1 (Figure 3H), and hence the strong electrostatic feature of RhoD in that region is absent in RND1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and Figure 3G.

claim: The tight membrane interaction of RhoD may be attributed to the short C-terminal tail and to the positively charged surface patch.
source: These observations combined suggest that the tight membrane interaction of RhoD may be attributed to the short C-terminal tail and to the positively charged surface patch, which distinguish RhoD from RND1.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation and structural data.

claim: The short C-terminal tail and the positively charged surface patch distinguish RhoD from RND1.
source: These observations combined suggest that the tight membrane interaction of RhoD may be attributed to the short C-terminal tail and to the positively charged surface patch, which distinguish RhoD from RND1.
evidence: This is supported by sequence and structural analysis.

claim: In control simulations, the RND1 membrane contact area dwindled.
source: Indeed, in the control simulations, the RND1 membrane contact area dwindled, while the RhoD membrane contact area grew steadily and gradually surpassed the RND1 (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: In control simulations, the RhoD membrane contact area grew steadily and gradually surpassed the RND1.
source: Indeed, in the control simulations, the RND1 membrane contact area dwindled, while the RhoD membrane contact area grew steadily and gradually surpassed the RND1 (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: In the plexin dimer, each RhoD or RND1 molecule is located in a space confined by the membrane and the RBD domain and interacts with both simultaneously.
source: In the plexin dimer, each RhoD or RND1 molecule is located in a space confined by the membrane and the RBD domain and interacts with both simultaneously (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling and Figure 4A, B.

claim: In the simulations, the RBD interacts with either RhoD or RND1 stably.
source: In the simulations, the RBD interacts with either RhoD or RND1 stably, although RhoD interacts with RBD with a slightly larger interface than RND1 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RhoD interacts with RBD with a slightly larger interface than RND1.
source: In the simulations, the RBD interacts with either RhoD or RND1 stably, although RhoD interacts with RBD with a slightly larger interface than RND1 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The RBD domain appeared to be inherently flexible with respect to the GAP domain as shown in the monomer simulations.
source: The RBD domain appeared to be inherently flexible with respect to the GAP domain as shown in the monomer simulations (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The RBD domain exhibited substantial flexibility with respect to the GAP domain in existing crystal structures of plexins.
source: This is suggested by existing crystal structures of plexins, in which the RBD domain exhibited substantial flexibility with respect to the GAP domain (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and Figure 4F.

claim: The interface between RBD and GAP appeared to be reduced by the presence of RhoD but not by the presence of RND1.
source: The interface between RBD and GAP appeared to be reduced by the presence of RhoD but not by the presence of RND1 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, E).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, E.

claim: The RBD RMSD with respect to its initial position was overall larger for the RhoD-bound than for the RND1-bound plexin dimer.
source: The RBD RMSD with respect to its initial position was overall larger for the RhoD-bound than for the RND1-bound plexin dimer (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that RhoD likely displaces the RBD from its native position while RND1 tends to stabilize RBD at that position.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RhoD likely displaces the RBD from its native position while RND1 tends to stabilize RBD at that position.
source: The RBD RMSD with respect to its initial position was overall larger for the RhoD-bound than for the RND1-bound plexin dimer (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating that RhoD likely displaces the RBD from its native position while RND1 tends to stabilize RBD at that position.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: The differential RBD positioning and dynamics may likely be attributable to the differential membrane interactions of RND1 and RhoD.
source: Since RBD binds stably with both RND1 and RhoD, the differential RBD positioning and dynamics may likely be attributable to the differential membrane interactions of RND1 and RhoD.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: The dimerization of plexins is mediated by their dimerization helices that are immediately C-terminal to the juxtamembrane helices.
source: The dimerization of plexins is mediated by their dimerization helices that are immediately C-terminal to the juxtamembrane helices (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and Figure 1B.

claim: The interaction between two dimerization helices in the dimer is reinforced by Helix 11 of the GAP domain.
source: The interaction between two dimerization helices in the dimer, which resembles coiled-coil interactions, is reinforced by Helix 11 of the GAP domain (Figure 1C; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: In crystal structures, Helix 11 is a stable helix.
source: In crystal structures, Helix 11 is a stable helix, but the segment to its N-terminal is more variable structurally – it takes the form of a 310 or an α helix in some crystal structures, but in many other structures it is disordered.
evidence: This is supported by structural data.

claim: The segment N-terminal to Helix 11 is more variable structurally.
source: In crystal structures, Helix 11 is a stable helix, but the segment to its N-terminal is more variable structurally – it takes the form of a 310 or an α helix in some crystal structures, but in many other structures it is disordered.
evidence: This is supported by structural data.

claim: When the segment N-terminal to Helix 11 is a 310 or an α helix, it becomes an extension of Helix 11 and runs adjacent and in parallel to the dimerization helix.
source: When it is a 310 or an α helix, it becomes an extension of Helix 11 and runs adjacent and in parallel to the dimerization helix, structurally reinforcing the interaction of the two dimerization helices in resemblance to a buttress.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The buttress segment structurally reinforces the interaction of the two dimerization helices.
source: When it is a 310 or an α helix, it becomes an extension of Helix 11 and runs adjacent and in parallel to the dimerization helix, structurally reinforcing the interaction of the two dimerization helices in resemblance to a buttress.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The RBD is connected to the plexin GAP domain by two linkers, a C-terminal and an N-terminal linker.
source: The RBD is connected to the plexin GAP domain by two linkers, a C-terminal and an N-terminal linker.
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge.

claim: The C-terminal linker is followed immediately by the buttress segment.
source: The C-terminal linker (residues 1597–1662) is followed immediately by the buttress segment.
evidence: This is supported by structural data.

claim: The C-terminal linker is long and partially disordered in crystal structures.
source: This linker is long and partially disordered in crystal structures, especially in the part closer to the buttress segment.
evidence: This is supported by structural data.

claim: The C-terminal linker is conformationally highly flexible.
source: This suggests that this linker is conformationally highly flexible.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural disorder.

claim: The N-terminal linker connects RBD to the bulk of the GAP domain and is packed against the buttress segment.
source: The shorter N-terminal linker (residues 1482–1495) connects RBD to the bulk of the GAP domain and is packed against the buttress segment (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and Figure 5A, B.

claim: The N and C linkers mediate the regulation of the buttress segment by the RBD.
source: It is likely that the N and C linkers mediate the regulation of the buttress segment by the RBD since their conformations are expected to be closely coupled with the position of the RBD on one side and with the conformation of the buttress segment on the other.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The buttress interaction with the dimerization helix is minimal in a monomeric plexin.
source: Our simulations showed that the buttress interaction with the dimerization helix is minimal in a monomeric plexin, and this interaction increases substantially in plexin dimers (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The buttress interaction with the dimerization helix increases substantially in plexin dimers.
source: Our simulations showed that the buttress interaction with the dimerization helix is minimal in a monomeric plexin, and this interaction increases substantially in plexin dimers (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: With RhoD binding at the RBD, the buttress interaction with the dimerization helix in the plexin dimer is much reduced compared to that in the RND1-bound dimer or in the dimer where the RBD domains are unoccupied.
source: Importantly, with RhoD binding at the RBD, the buttress interaction with the dimerization helix in the plexin dimer is much reduced compared to that in the RND1-bound dimer or in the dimer where the RBD domains are unoccupied, suggesting that RhoD weakens the buttress interaction with the dimerization helix and potentially destabilizes the plexin dimer.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: RhoD weakens the buttress interaction with the dimerization helix and potentially destabilizes the plexin dimer.
source: Importantly, with RhoD binding at the RBD, the buttress interaction with the dimerization helix in the plexin dimer is much reduced compared to that in the RND1-bound dimer or in the dimer where the RBD domains are unoccupied, suggesting that RhoD weakens the buttress interaction with the dimerization helix and potentially destabilizes the plexin dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: In simulations of the RhoD-bound plexin dimer, the buttress segment lost its helical structure and gradually disengaged the dimerization helices.
source: In simulations of the RhoD-bound plexin dimer, the buttress segment lost its helical structure and gradually disengaged the dimerization helices (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 5C.

claim: In simulations of the RND1-bound dimer both the helical structure and the interaction with the dimerization helices are much more stable.
source: In contrast, in simulations of the RND1-bound dimer both the helical structure and the interaction with the dimerization helices are much more stable (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 5B.

claim: The contact area of the buttress segments and the dimerization helices is smaller in the RhoD-bound system than in the RND1-bound system.
source: The difference is reflected by the smaller contact area of the buttress segments and the dimerization helices in the RhoD-bound system than in the RND1-bound system (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the RhoD-bound dimer the pair of the dimerization helices was conformationally more variable than that in an RBD-unoccupied plexin dimer.
source: Moreover, the simulations showed that in the RhoD-bound dimer the pair of the dimerization helices was conformationally more variable than that in an RBD-unoccupied plexin dimer, and the dimerization helices in an RND1-bound dimer were less variable than the unoccupied dimer (Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The dimerization helices in an RND1-bound dimer were less variable than the unoccupied dimer.
source: Moreover, the simulations showed that in the RhoD-bound dimer the pair of the dimerization helices was conformationally more variable than that in an RBD-unoccupied plexin dimer, and the dimerization helices in an RND1-bound dimer were less variable than the unoccupied dimer (Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data and Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RhoD binding destabilizes the plexin dimerization interface while RND1 binding may stabilize the dimer.
source: This is consistent with the notion that RhoD binding destabilizes the plexin dimerization interface while RND1 binding may stabilize the dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: The differential membrane interaction of RND1 and RhoD propagates to the plexin dimerization interface through the RBD domain and its N and C linkers.
source: Based on these simulation results, we suggest that the differential membrane interaction of RND1 and RhoD propagates to the plexin dimerization interface and confers antithetic impact to plexin dimerization through the RBD domain and its N and C linkers (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data and Figure 5B.

claim: RhoD binding destabilizes the RBD with respect to the GAP domain, destabilizing the buttress segment with respect to the dimerization interface, and ultimately leads to destabilization of the dimer interface.
source: RhoD binding destabilizes the RBD with respect to the GAP domain, destabilizing the buttress segment with respect to the dimerization interface, and ultimately leads to destabilization of the dimer interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: By the same RBD-centered route, RND1 binding helps stabilize the plexin dimer.
source: In contrast, by the same RBD-centered route, RND1 binding helps stabilize the plexin dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: Plexins function in ways similar to a transistor in that they take two inputs and their responses to the primary input of semaphorin are regulated by the secondary input in the form of the Rho-family regulatory GTPase binding at the RBD domain.
source: Plexins function in ways similar to a transistor in that they take two inputs and their responses to the primary input of semaphorin are regulated by the secondary input in the form of the Rho-family regulatory GTPase binding at the RBD domain.
evidence: This is an analogy based on functional understanding.

claim: The differential effects of RND1 and RhoD may arise from their differential interactions with the membrane.
source: Our structural and molecular dynamics simulations and analyses suggest that the differential effects of RND1 and RhoD may arise from their differential interactions with the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation and structural data.

claim: The antithetic roles of RND1 and RhoD result from two seemingly minor differences: RhoD furnishes a much shorter C-terminal tail than RND1, and RhoD features a surface region that is rich in positively charged residue.
source: We show that the antithetic roles of RND1 and RhoD result from two seemingly minor differences. First, RhoD furnishes a much shorter C-terminal tail than RND1, and consequently, RhoD is spatially more restrained to the membrane than RND1. Secondly, RhoD features a surface region that is rich in positively charged residue, which serves as the interface with membranes; these positively charged residues are not present in RND1.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation and structural data.

claim: RhoD is spatially more restrained to the membrane than RND1.
source: First, RhoD furnishes a much shorter C-terminal tail than RND1, and consequently, RhoD is spatially more restrained to the membrane than RND1.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation data.

claim: The positively charged residues that serve as the membrane interface in RhoD are not present in RND1.
source: Secondly, RhoD features a surface region that is rich in positively charged residue, which serves as the interface with membranes; these positively charged residues are not present in RND1.
evidence: This is supported by sequence and structural analysis.

claim: Mutating RND1 residues at the αI or α4 helices into positively charged arginines or lysines should impair the role of RND1 as a plexin activator.
source: Specifically, mutating RND1 residues (e.g., Leu133, Glu138, Ser140, and Glu150) at the αI or α4 helices (the putative membrane-contacting region of RhoD) into positively charged arginines or lysines should impair the role of RND1 as a plexin activator, and conversely, mutating the lysines and arginines at these two helices of RhoD should impair the role of RhoD as a plexin inhibitor.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Mutating the lysines and arginines at the αI or α4 helices of RhoD should impair the role of RhoD as a plexin inhibitor.
source: Specifically, mutating RND1 residues (e.g., Leu133, Glu138, Ser140, and Glu150) at the αI or α4 helices (the putative membrane-contacting region of RhoD) into positively charged arginines or lysines should impair the role of RND1 as a plexin activator, and conversely, mutating the lysines and arginines at these two helices of RhoD should impair the role of RhoD as a plexin inhibitor.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Lengthening the C-terminal loop of RhoD should impair its inhibitory effect.
source: By the same rationale, lengthening the C-terminal loop of RhoD should impair its inhibitory effect, while shortening the loop of RND1 should impair its activating effect.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Shortening the loop of RND1 should impair its activating effect.
source: By the same rationale, lengthening the C-terminal loop of RhoD should impair its inhibitory effect, while shortening the loop of RND1 should impair its activating effect.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The two features (short C-terminal tail and positively charged membrane interface) are correlated among Rho-family GTPases.
source: We analyzed the sequences of the Rho-family GTPases and, to our surprise, found that these two features are indeed correlated. The Rho GTPases with shorter C-terminal tails indeed tend to feature more positively charged residues at the putative membrane interface (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and Figure 6.

claim: Rho GTPases with shorter C-terminal tails tend to feature more positively charged residues at the putative membrane interface.
source: The Rho GTPases with shorter C-terminal tails indeed tend to feature more positively charged residues at the putative membrane interface (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and Figure 6.

claim: Other Rho-family GTPases may also be involved in regulations of plexin signaling.
source: This suggests that, besides RND1 and RhoD, other Rho-family GTPases may also be involved in regulations of plexin signaling, and that the Rho-family GTPases with short C-terminal tails may likely be downregulators and the other with long C-terminal tails likely upregulators.
evidence: This is a speculation based on sequence analysis.

claim: Rho-family GTPases with short C-terminal tails may likely be downregulators of plexin.
source: This suggests that, besides RND1 and RhoD, other Rho-family GTPases may also be involved in regulations of plexin signaling, and that the Rho-family GTPases with short C-terminal tails may likely be downregulators and the other with long C-terminal tails likely upregulators.
evidence: This is a speculation based on sequence analysis and the proposed mechanism.

claim: Rho-family GTPases with long C-terminal tails may likely be upregulators of plexin.
source: This suggests that, besides RND1 and RhoD, other Rho-family GTPases may also be involved in regulations of plexin signaling, and that the Rho-family GTPases with short C-terminal tails may likely be downregulators and the other with long C-terminal tails likely upregulators.
evidence: This is a speculation based on sequence analysis and the proposed mechanism.

claim: The findings raise the question as to whether downregulation associated with RhoD binding may be a part of a negative feedback mechanism for plexin signaling involving the PI3K/AKT pathway.
source: Our findings raise the question as to whether downregulation associated with RhoD binding may be a part of a negative feedback mechanism for plexin signaling involving the PI3K/AKT pathway.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and known signaling pathways.

claim: Plexin signaling activates the PI3K/AKT pathway, upon which PIP2 lipids in the membrane are phosphorylated and converted to more negatively charged PIP3 lipids.
source: There are reports that plexin signaling activates the PI3K/AKT pathway, upon which PIP2 lipids in the membrane are phosphorylated and converted to more negatively charged PIP3 lipids (Falkenburger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Falkenburger et al., 2010.

claim: In a membrane environment of a high composition of negatively charged lipids such as POPS, PIP2, and PIP3, plexin signaling is likely more susceptible to negative regulation by RhoD.
source: In a membrane environment of a high composition of negatively charged lipids such as POPS, PIP2, and PIP3, plexin signaling is likely more susceptible to negative regulation by RhoD.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings about RhoD membrane interaction.

claim: A recent study on plexin B1 identified the functional importance of the buttress segment based on analysis of plexin enzymatic turnover.
source: Reassuringly, our findings are supported by a recent study on plexin B1, which (Li et al., 2021) identified the functional importance of the buttress segment (or 'activation switch loop' as is referred therein) based on analysis of plexin enzymatic turnover, and showed that the segment helps stabilize the dimerization helix when the plexin active site is occupied by Rap.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: The buttress segment helps stabilize the dimerization helix when the plexin active site is occupied by Rap.
source: Reassuringly, our findings are supported by a recent study on plexin B1, which (Li et al., 2021) identified the functional importance of the buttress segment (or 'activation switch loop' as is referred therein) based on analysis of plexin enzymatic turnover, and showed that the segment helps stabilize the dimerization helix when the plexin active site is occupied by Rap.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2021.
